title: AI Finds Six Ways to 3D-Print a NASA Rocket Alloy That Had Stumped Engineers for Years
excerpt: Washington State University researchers used artificial intelligence to test just 40 of more than 100 million possible configurations, discovering settings that allow a high-performance copper alloy to be printed on standard commercial equipment for the first time.
body:
• WSU researchers used AI to identify six successful 3D-printing configurations for GRCop-42, a NASA-developed copper alloy used in rocket engines, out of more than 100 million possibilities — testing just 40.
  • The team achieved the first successful print of the alloy at 500 watts, low enough for standard commercial printers that could not handle it before.
  • The work, published in the Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, won the Innovative Deployed Application Award.
  • Indian-origin researchers Amit Bandyopadhyay, Susmita Bose, and Jana Doppa played key roles in the project, which could extend to drug discovery and other fields.

A team at Washington State University has used artificial intelligence to crack a manufacturing problem that had resisted brute-force approaches for years: how to 3D-print a high-performance NASA alloy on ordinary commercial equipment. The breakthrough, achieved through just 40 targeted experiments out of more than 100 million possible configurations, could open access to a material previously restricted to specialized labs.

The research, published in the Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, also received the Innovative Deployed Application Award at the organization's annual conference.

A Needle in 100 Million Haystacks

The alloy in question, GRCop-42, is a copper-chromium-niobium blend developed by NASA for extreme-heat environments. It is used in liquid rocket engine combustion chambers because it can withstand punishing temperatures while efficiently conducting heat. But printing it has required so much laser power that roughly 90 percent of commercial 3D printers cannot handle the job.

https://x.com/EvanKirstel/status/2093545425353794032

Each printing attempt costs hundreds of dollars in materials and can take days to analyze. Testing every possible combination of settings — laser power, speed, layer thickness, and other parameters — was never realistic.

"Ninety percent of commercial printers cannot print this metal alloy, so given that we were able to find these feasible process parameters, it allows us to use those commercial printers, and we are essentially democratizing the printing of this alloy."

— Jana Doppa, Huie-Rogers Endowed Chair Professor of Computer Science, WSU

How the AI Approach Worked

The team, led by Professor Jana Doppa from WSU's School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, started with data from 37 printing configurations that had already failed in earlier experiments. They built an AI model that estimated which untested combinations of settings were most likely to succeed.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=FqZTQA6p7Tc

Rather than chasing only the most promising-looking options, the AI balanced two priorities. Some experiments targeted configurations that appeared likely to work, while others explored uncertain territory to improve the model's understanding of the search space.

"Sometimes they printed a certain configuration, and the product just melted," said Azza Fadhel, the paper's first author and a PhD student in computer science. "It wasn't really printable, and even with time and money, they wouldn't be able to try all 100 million options."

Over three months, the AI-guided process identified six successful configurations at different laser power levels. For the first time, the team printed GRCop-42 at just 500 watts — well within the range of standard commercial equipment.

Indian-Origin Researchers Drive the Breakthrough

The cross-disciplinary team included several Indian-origin researchers. Professors Susmita Bose and Amit Bandyopadhyay from WSU's School of Mechanical and Materials Engineering led the materials science side, working with Nathaniel Zuckschwerdt to print and evaluate the alloy samples using configurations chosen by the AI. Aryan Deshwal from the University of Minnesota also collaborated on the project.

"They would give me back the results, and I liked all of them — even if they failed — because every result improved our AI model," Fadhel said.

Beyond Rockets

Printing GRCop-42 at lower power could reduce energy consumption, decrease equipment wear, and lower post-processing costs. More importantly, it could put the alloy within reach of universities, smaller laboratories, and companies that lack access to high-power printing systems.

The researchers say the same AI framework could be adapted to find workable processing conditions for other metal alloys and additive manufacturing systems. Beyond manufacturing, the method could help tackle scientific problems in drug discovery and other fields where successful outcomes are rare and experiments are expensive.

"There's always uncertainty when you are deploying something where real people, materials, and physical costs are involved," Doppa said. "We didn't know whether we would succeed or not, and there is always that risk. There are real stakes. I was very surprised that we were able to do this so well."
